summary: Specifies PA-TNC, a posture attribute protocol identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-M 1.0. Devices use it to report their security health, and the document checks it against the Network Endpoint Assessment requirements. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Before entering a building, you answer a short health checklist, and this describes the form the questions and answers use.

questions: what is the noskip flag in pa-tnc
subtitle: The message format an endpoint uses to report its security posture, such as antivirus, firewall and OS details, during a network health check.

tldr.problem: A network that wants to check whether a device is healthy before admitting it needs a common, compact way for software on the device to report facts like product, version, firewall ports and status.
tldr.mechanism: PA-TNC defines a PA-TNC message with a small header followed by type-length-value attributes. Standard attribute types cover product, version, status, ports, packages, results, remediation and errors, and vendors can add their own under their Private Enterprise Number.
tldr.outcome: PA-TNC is identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-M 1.0 and is checked against the NEA requirements in an appendix. It relies on the layers below it for authentication and integrity.

today: RFC 5792 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2010, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It works together with PB-TNC in RFC 5793 and the NEA requirements in RFC 5209.

sections.title: What PA-TNC Is
sections.content:
RFC 5792 specifies PA-TNC, a Posture Attribute protocol that is identical to the Trusted Computing Group's IF-M 1.0 protocol. It then evaluates PA-TNC against the requirements in the Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) Overview and Requirements document, RFC 5209.

The RFC does not define an architecture. It defines a protocol that works inside the NEA reference model, and it assumes the reader already knows that model. PA-TNC messages are carried inside the PB-TNC protocol, specified in RFC 5793.

The two parties are Posture Collectors on the endpoint, which gather facts about a component such as an anti-virus product, and Posture Validators on the server side, which check those facts against policy.
sections.eli5: On your side, a helper writes down facts about your device. On the network's side, a checker reads them and decides whether they are good enough. This RFC is the form they both use.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
The design rests on three ideas. First, a standard namespace of component types and attributes lets open source and vendor products work together under one policy. Second, a vendor namespace lets vendors add new attributes quickly, because the endpoint environment changes fast. Every namespace is identified by an SMI Private Enterprise Number (PEN), also called a vendor ID, where 0 means the IETF.

Third, attributes use binary type-length-value (TLV) encoding rather than text such as XML. The RFC gives efficiency as the main reason: less bandwidth on slow or high-latency links, room inside transport protocols limited by packet size, and less CPU on low-power endpoints. Vendors may still put XML inside their own attributes, but software that knows only standard attributes will treat those as opaque.

Collectors and validators MUST NOT require support for particular vendor-specific types and MUST interoperate despite differences in which ones they support. Administrators MAY configure them to require specific ones.
sections.eli5: Everyone shares one standard list of questions, and companies can add their own extra questions on a separate page with their name on it. Answers are written in a short code to save space.

sections.title: Messaging Model and Subtypes
sections.content:
PA-TNC rides on PB-TNC, which gives a reliable, multi-round-trip exchange and a publish/subscribe delivery model. Collectors only send to validators and the reverse. There is no collector-to-collector or validator-to-validator messaging. PA-TNC itself does not know which transport lies below PB-TNC.

Routing depends on the PA message type, made of a PA Message Vendor ID and a PA Subtype. In this RFC the subtype names the type of component, so only parties registered for that component receive the message. Every attribute in a message MUST relate to the component named in its subtype. The IETF subtypes, used with vendor ID 0, are Testing (0), Operating System (1), Anti-Virus (2), Anti-Spyware (3), Anti-Malware (4), Firewall (5), IDPS (6), VPN (7) and NEA Client (8).

When a collector reports on several implementations of one component, such as two VPN products, it gets a separate Posture Collector Identifier for each and sends one message per implementation. That lets the receiver tell which attributes describe the same product. A validator that wants a specific collector, for example to send remediation, can use PB-TNC's exclusive delivery.
sections.eli5: Each question sheet is labeled Antivirus, Firewall and so on, and goes only to the people who handle that topic. If you have two firewalls, each gets its own sheet.

sections.title: Message and Attribute Headers
sections.content:
Every PA-TNC message starts with an 8-byte header: a Version byte, 3 reserved bytes and a 32-bit Message Identifier. Senders MUST set the version to 0x01. A recipient that does not support the version MUST reply with a Version Not Supported error as the only attribute in a version 1 message. The identifier lets a sender and recipient refer to a message in errors, and senders MUST NOT reuse one during an assessment.

Then come zero or more attributes. Each begins with the same header: an 8-bit Flags field, a 24-bit Vendor ID, a 32-bit Type and a 32-bit Length that covers the whole attribute including the header. The length MUST be at least 12, and a receiver can use it to skip attributes it does not know.

Bit 0 of the flags (0x80) is NOSKIP. If it is set and the receiver does not support the attribute, the receiver MUST NOT process any part of the message and SHOULD answer with an Attribute Type Not Supported error. If it is clear, unsupported attributes SHOULD simply be skipped. Vendor ID 0xffffff and type 0xffffffff are reserved and MUST NOT be sent. All attributes in one message MUST concern the same implementation of the component.
sections.eli5: Each message has a cover note with a number, and each answer has a label that says who defined it, what kind it is and how long it is. If a label says you must understand it and you do not, you stop.

sections.title: The Standard Attributes
sections.content:
Twelve standard attribute types exist, numbered 1 to 12 (0 is reserved for testing), always with vendor ID 0. Posture Validators send only some of them.

  • Attribute Request (1): a validator lists the attribute types it wants. A collector MAY send all, some or none, but MUST NOT send unrequested attributes other than errors.
  • Product Information (2): numeric vendor and product IDs plus a UTF-8 product name. Collectors for the standard subtypes MUST support sending it.
  • Numeric Version (3): major, minor, build and service pack numbers, so validators can compare versions.
  • String Version (4): version, build and configuration version as UTF-8 strings. Their syntax is left undefined because products differ.
  • Operational Status (5): whether the product is not installed, installed but not operational or operational, the result of its last use and a Last Use time. The time is a 20-octet RFC 3339 string in UTC.
  • Port Filter (6): protocol and port pairs with a blocked flag, so a firewall can list whichever of blocked or allowed ports is shorter. It MUST NOT mix blocked and allowed ports for one protocol.
  • Installed Packages (7): package names and versions, up to 65535 packages. It can be long, so collectors SHOULD NOT send it unless asked.
  • PA-TNC Error (8): see the error section.
  • Assessment Result (9): from a validator, one of five values from compliant (0) to unable to determine because of an error (3) or from the attributes provided (4).
  • Remediation Instructions (10): a URI (type 1) or a human-readable string with a language tag (type 2).
  • Forwarding Enabled (11): whether the endpoint forwards traffic between interfaces, which some networks treat as a risk.
  • Factory Default Password Enabled (12): whether a default password is still active.

Vendors can define more attributes under their own vendor ID. The RFC does not define any itself, and expects popular ones may later get standard equivalents.
sections.eli5: The standard form asks things like: what product is it, which version, is it running, which doors are open, and did you change the factory password. The checker can answer pass, fail or I cannot tell, and can send a how-to-fix note.

sections.title: Errors
sections.content:
The PA-TNC Error attribute carries an error code with its own vendor ID, plus error information whose format depends on the code. Three standard codes exist: Invalid Parameter (1), Version Not Supported (2) and Attribute Type Not Supported (3). Value 0 is reserved.

Each error echoes the offending message's version, reserved bytes and message identifier so the sender can tell which message failed. Invalid Parameter adds an offset to the bad value. Version Not Supported adds the maximum and minimum versions the sender supports, and the sender MUST support every version in that range. Attribute Type Not Supported adds a copy of the attribute's flags, vendor ID and type.

A party that receives a PA-TNC error MUST NOT answer with another error, because that could loop forever. It may log, adapt, ignore or end the assessment. Errors SHOULD be sent with the same subtype as the message that caused them, and with exclusive delivery where possible, so only the sender of the bad message sees them.
sections.eli5: If someone sends a garbled form, you send back a note saying which page and line was wrong. If they answer that note with another note, nobody would ever stop, so you never answer a note about a mistake.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
PA-TNC does not protect itself. It relies on the underlying transport (PT) for confidentiality, authentication, integrity and a freshness exchange, and it assumes the posture brokers deliver messages correctly and do not observe, alter or leak them. The RFC also lists what collectors and validators trust each other to do: collectors report accurately and validators request only what they need and do not send harmful remediation.

It walks through six threats: attribute theft by eavesdroppers, message fabrication, modification, replay of an earlier compliant assessment, insertion of extra attributes, and denial of service. One example is a forged Remediation URI that a collector follows automatically. Collectors SHOULD NOT blindly follow remediation instructions and should validate risky actions, for example by asking the user.

On privacy, the protocol is meant for controlled disclosure. Messages cover only security-related components, and standard attributes are generic rather than user-specific. The RFC suggests collectors offer a privacy filter by target network, and warns that a user who shares less may fail an assessment and be denied access.
sections.eli5: The form itself has no lock, so it must travel in a locked bag, or someone could swap your answers or reuse an old good report. And you may want to tell the school less than you tell your family.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC creates three IANA registries: PA-TNC Attribute Types, PA-TNC Error Codes and PA-TNC Remediation Parameters Types. It also adds the nine PA Subtypes, 0 to 8, to the PA Subtypes registry defined for PB-TNC. Each registry holds IETF values (vendor ID 0) and vendor-defined values, with vendors encouraged but not required to register theirs.

New values are added by Expert Review with Specification Required under RFC 5226. The designated experts are told not to worry about running out of numbers, since roughly 2^32 are available to the IETF and to each vendor. Instead they should require a permanent, public specification, clear definitions that aid interoperability, and discourage similar but incompatible values.
sections.eli5: A public notebook keeps the official list of question numbers. A person checks that each new entry is written up clearly before adding it.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: MUST be 0x01 for messages that follow this RFC.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 on transmission, ignored on reception.

fields.name: Message Identifier
fields.desc: Unique per sender within an assessment; echoed in errors.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 0 (0x80) is NOSKIP; bits 1 to 7 are reserved.

fields.name: Attribute Vendor ID
fields.desc: Owner of the type namespace; 0 for IETF standard types.

fields.name: Attribute Length
fields.desc: Octets in the whole attribute including this header; at least 12.
